doc.title: Daryl Sherman interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 11, 2024

title: Reading the lunchtime crowd and choosing songs
summary: She plays Fats Waller, American Songbook and light tunes for passers-by, and mentions long solo piano and hotel gigs.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: I started playing as much Fats Waller as I could, and I have a few things that — I knew Dick Wellstood and I know enough about stride playing to know that I could never pull it off, it’s just too many notes and you know, too much precision. And — but later on he was really getting into the American Songbook and he brought songbooks with him. I used to go hear him a lot. And Sinatra. And particularly in this day and age post- pandemic and whatever, it’s kind of a challenge insofar as just bringing people back to the office during the day. So many people are working from home and you know, clearly there are people who are still in the office but not as many as there used to be. And it’s — you just never know who’s — oh and the reason I didn’t even realize how many atriums there were, particularly in this area, that had a piano I guess for the reason that it’s the owner’s way of giving back to the City because they got a tax break to build that building and there’s a public restroom, they’ve got a Starbucks, you know they do provide some table and chairs and in some cases a live person. But what I do now is, as you said, kind of case out who’s there and just the vibe. Even though I start at twelve I start with [sings] “Oh What a Beautiful Morning” and I go to, “I Love Being Here with You.” And other things I do for the most part these people are so young now they don’t really know from Peggy Lee necessarily, but I do notice that they know “From the Vine” or just something lilting. And I’m not singing. This is — at first this was kind of the hardest part for me. I’ve done solo piano gigs and I’ve done long term hotel gigs. Fourteen years at The Waldorf. On and off probably about the same amount of time at The Sheridan Center. And I know when you can just sit and be a jazz player and I know when you have to play to the audience, which is fine because it’s a way of relating and building relationships and it’s the best way to build a repertoire. I’m having fun. When I see people walk in [sings] “Walk right in, sit right down. Baby let —”
